cholinergic-drugs.moa: Agonists stimulate muscarinic (and nicotinic) receptors directly; Anticholinesterases block acetylcholinesterase so acetylcholine builds up at synapses
cholinergic-drugs.uses: Glaucoma (pilocarpine); urinary retention and paralytic ileus (bethanechol, neostigmine); myasthenia gravis (neostigmine, pyridostigmine); reversal of neuromuscular block; Alzheimer's disease (donepezil, rivastigmine)
cholinergic-drugs.adr: Salivation, lacrimation, sweating, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps; bradycardia and hypotension; bronchospasm; miosis; muscle weakness in overdose (cholinergic crisis)
cholinergic-drugs.ci: Bronchial asthma and COPD; peptic ulcer; intestinal or urinary obstruction; bradycardia and heart block; hyperthyroidism; Parkinsonism

anticholinergic-drugs.moa: Competitively block muscarinic receptors, so the parasympathetic effects of acetylcholine are lost
anticholinergic-drugs.uses: Preanaesthetic medication to dry secretions; mydriasis and cycloplegia for eye examination; antispasmodic in colic; bronchodilator in COPD (ipratropium, tiotropium); overactive bladder; Parkinsonism; motion sickness (hyoscine); organophosphate poisoning (atropine)
anticholinergic-drugs.adr: Dry mouth, blurred vision, photophobia, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, flushing, hot dry skin; confusion and delirium in the elderly or at high dose
anticholinergic-drugs.ci: Angle-closure glaucoma; prostatic hypertrophy; paralytic ileus and pyloric obstruction; tachyarrhythmias; caution in elderly people with dementia

ganglionic-stimulants.moa: Nicotine stimulates nicotinic receptors at autonomic ganglia and the adrenal medulla, releasing noradrenaline and adrenaline; lobeline acts in a similar way
ganglionic-stimulants.uses: Nicotine replacement for smoking cessation; otherwise no clinical use; lobeline was once used as a respiratory stimulant
ganglionic-stimulants.adr: Nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, raised blood pressure, tremor, sweating; high doses cause convulsions and respiratory paralysis
ganglionic-stimulants.ci: Recent myocardial infarction, unstable angina and severe arrhythmias; peptic ulcer; vasospastic disease; caution in pregnancy

ganglionic-blocking-agents.moa: Block nicotinic receptors in both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, so the result depends on which tone dominates in each organ
ganglionic-blocking-agents.uses: Hardly used today; trimethaphan for controlled hypotension in surgery and hypertensive emergencies; mecamylamine rarely in severe hypertension
ganglionic-blocking-agents.adr: Postural hypotension, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, impotence, paralytic ileus
ganglionic-blocking-agents.ci: Glaucoma; urinary or intestinal obstruction; coronary or cerebrovascular insufficiency; renal impairment

adrenergic-drugs.moa: Stimulate α and β receptors directly, release noradrenaline (indirect), or both (mixed); α1 causes vasoconstriction, β1 cardiac stimulation, β2 bronchodilation and uterine relaxation
adrenergic-drugs.uses: Anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest (adrenaline); shock and hypotension (noradrenaline, dopamine, dobutamine); asthma (salbutamol, terbutaline); nasal decongestion (oxymetazoline, xylometazoline); mydriasis (phenylephrine); preterm labour (ritodrine)
adrenergic-drugs.adr: Anxiety, tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, arrhythmias, hypertension, headache; tissue necrosis if noradrenaline or dopamine leaks out of a vein; rebound congestion with nasal decongestants
adrenergic-drugs.ci: Hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmias and hyperthyroidism; halothane anaesthesia (arrhythmias); MAO inhibitor use (pressor crisis); angle-closure glaucoma

alpha-adrenergic-blocking-drugs.moa: Block α receptors; phenoxybenzamine blocks irreversibly and the others competitively; α1 block relaxes vascular and prostatic smooth muscle
alpha-adrenergic-blocking-drugs.uses: Phaeochromocytoma (phenoxybenzamine, phentolamine); benign prostatic hyperplasia (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, silodosin); hypertension (prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin); Raynaud's phenomenon
alpha-adrenergic-blocking-drugs.adr: First-dose postural hypotension, dizziness, reflex tachycardia, nasal stuffiness, fluid retention, failure of ejaculation; floppy iris syndrome in cataract surgery (tamsulosin)
alpha-adrenergic-blocking-drugs.ci: Coronary artery disease and recent MI (non-selective drugs); severe renal impairment; hypersensitivity; caution in the elderly because of falls

beta-adrenergic-blocking-drugs.moa: Competitively block β receptors; β1 block lowers heart rate, contractility and renin release; β2 block causes bronchoconstriction
beta-adrenergic-blocking-drugs.uses: Hypertension; angina; arrhythmias; post-MI and heart failure (metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol); migraine prophylaxis; thyrotoxicosis symptoms; glaucoma (timolol); anxiety tremors; variceal bleeding prophylaxis
beta-adrenergic-blocking-drugs.adr: Bradycardia, heart block, fatigue, cold extremities, bronchospasm, masking of hypoglycaemia, vivid dreams, depression, impotence; rebound on sudden withdrawal
beta-adrenergic-blocking-drugs.ci: Bronchial asthma and COPD; second or third degree heart block; sick sinus syndrome; acute decompensated heart failure; severe peripheral vascular disease; caution in diabetes treated with insulin

beta-adrenergic-blocking-drugs-2.moa: The same β-receptor blockade, grouped by generation: first nonselective (β1 and β2), second cardioselective (β1), third with an extra vasodilating action (α1 block or nitric oxide release)
beta-adrenergic-blocking-drugs-2.uses: First generation: hypertension, angina, migraine, tremor; second: preferred in asthmatics and diabetics, MI and heart failure; third: hypertension, heart failure (carvedilol), hypertensive emergencies (labetalol)
beta-adrenergic-blocking-drugs-2.adr: Less bronchospasm and metabolic effect with cardioselective drugs, but bradycardia and fatigue remain; third generation: postural hypotension
beta-adrenergic-blocking-drugs-2.ci: Asthma (avoid nonselective drugs), heart block, severe bradycardia, decompensated heart failure

topical-drugs-for-glaucoma.moa: Lower intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous humour production (β-blockers, α2 agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) or by increasing outflow (prostaglandin analogues, miotics)
topical-drugs-for-glaucoma.uses: Open-angle glaucoma; ocular hypertension; miotics and osmotic agents also in acute angle-closure
topical-drugs-for-glaucoma.adr: β-blockers: bradycardia, bronchospasm; prostaglandins: iris darkening, eyelash growth, conjunctival redness; miotics: miosis, brow ache; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: stinging, bitter taste; α2 agonists: allergy, dry mouth
topical-drugs-for-glaucoma.ci: Timolol: asthma and heart block; pilocarpine: iritis and asthma; brimonidine: infants; prostaglandin analogues: caution in uveitis and macular oedema

histaminergic-agonists.moa: Histamine acts on H1 (smooth muscle contraction, vasodilation, itching), H2 (gastric acid secretion), H3 (presynaptic inhibition) and H4 receptors
histaminergic-agonists.uses: Mostly diagnostic, for example histamine to test gastric acid secretion; betahistine (H1 agonist and H3 antagonist) in Meniere's disease and vertigo
histaminergic-agonists.adr: Flushing, headache, hypotension, tachycardia, bronchospasm, gastric upset
histaminergic-agonists.ci: Bronchial asthma, peptic ulcer, hypotension, phaeochromocytoma (histamine test)

h1-antagonists.moa: Competitively block H1 receptors; first-generation drugs also block muscarinic, serotonin and α receptors and enter the brain
h1-antagonists.uses: Allergic rhinitis, urticaria and itching; motion sickness and vertigo (promethazine, dimenhydrinate); preanaesthetic sedation; cough and cold preparations; nausea of pregnancy; insomnia
h1-antagonists.adr: First generation: sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention; second generation (cetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine): little sedation; terfenadine and astemizole caused QT prolongation
h1-antagonists.ci: Driving or machinery (sedating drugs); angle-closure glaucoma; prostatic hypertrophy; asthma attack (thickens secretions); newborns and premature infants; with alcohol or sedatives

5-hydroxy-tryptamine-antagonists.moa: Block serotonin receptors: 5-HT2 antagonists (cyproheptadine, ketanserin), 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron) and nonselective ergot-type drugs (methysergide)
5-hydroxy-tryptamine-antagonists.uses: Ondansetron and granisetron: chemotherapy, radiotherapy and postoperative vomiting; cyproheptadine: allergy, appetite stimulant and serotonin syndrome; methysergide: migraine prophylaxis (rarely, because of fibrosis)
5-hydroxy-tryptamine-antagonists.adr: Headache, constipation, dizziness; QT prolongation (ondansetron); cyproheptadine: sedation and weight gain; methysergide: retroperitoneal fibrosis
5-hydroxy-tryptamine-antagonists.ci: Long QT syndrome (5-HT3 blockers); cyproheptadine in glaucoma and in neonates; methysergide in vascular disease and pregnancy

drugs-for-migraine.moa: Acute attack: triptans stimulate 5-HT1B/1D receptors, constricting cranial vessels and reducing CGRP release; ergotamine acts on 5-HT1 and α receptors; NSAIDs block prostaglandins; Prophylaxis: β-blockers, flunarizine, topiramate, valproate and amitriptyline reduce attack frequency
drugs-for-migraine.uses: Triptans (sumatriptan, rizatriptan) and ergotamine to abort attacks; antiemetics (metoclopramide, domperidone) alongside; propranolol, flunarizine and topiramate to prevent attacks
drugs-for-migraine.adr: Triptans: chest tightness, tingling, dizziness, flushing; ergotamine: nausea, vomiting, vasospasm, gangrene, medication-overuse headache; propranolol: bradycardia and fatigue
drugs-for-migraine.ci: Triptans and ergots: ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic or basilar migraine, and pregnancy (ergots); never combine a triptan with ergotamine within 24 hours

prostaglandins.moa: Act on specific prostanoid receptors: PGE2 and PGE1 contract the uterus, ripen the cervix, protect the gastric mucosa and keep the ductus arteriosus open; PGI2 (prostacyclin) vasodilates and inhibits platelets; PGF2α contracts the uterus and lowers intraocular pressure
prostaglandins.uses: Misoprostol: NSAID ulcer prevention, medical abortion, labour induction and postpartum haemorrhage; dinoprostone: cervical ripening; carboprost: postpartum haemorrhage; alprostadil: keeps the ductus open in neonates and treats erectile dysfunction; epoprostenol: pulmonary hypertension; latanoprost: glaucoma
prostaglandins.adr: Diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, nausea, uterine hypercontraction, fever, flushing, hypotension; apnoea in neonates (alprostadil)
prostaglandins.ci: Pregnancy (misoprostol for ulcers); previous caesarean or uterine scar for labour induction; asthma (PGF2α); cardiac disease with hypotension

nonsteroidal-antiinflammatory-drugs-anti.moa: Inhibit cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), lowering prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis; COX-2 selective drugs spare gastric COX-1; paracetamol acts mainly in the CNS and has weak anti-inflammatory effect
nonsteroidal-antiinflammatory-drugs-anti.uses: Pain, fever and inflammation; osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis; dysmenorrhoea; gout (indomethacin, naproxen); low-dose aspirin as an antiplatelet; patent ductus closure (indomethacin, ibuprofen); paracetamol as a safe antipyretic
nonsteroidal-antiinflammatory-drugs-anti.adr: Gastric irritation, ulcers and bleeding; renal impairment and fluid retention; bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma; platelet inhibition and bleeding; COX-2 drugs: cardiovascular thrombotic events; paracetamol overdose: liver necrosis; aspirin in children: Reye's syndrome
nonsteroidal-antiinflammatory-drugs-anti.ci: Peptic ulcer and GI bleeding; aspirin-induced asthma; renal failure and heart failure; late pregnancy (closes the ductus); bleeding disorders; children with viral fever (aspirin); COX-2 inhibitors in ischaemic heart disease and stroke; sulfonamide allergy (celecoxib)

antirheumatoid-drugs.moa: DMARDs slow the disease by different actions: methotrexate (folate antagonist), sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide (blocks pyrimidine synthesis), gold, penicillamine, and TNF-α blockers (etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab); NSAIDs and steroids give symptom relief
antirheumatoid-drugs.uses: Rheumatoid arthritis; some are also used in psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and other autoimmune diseases
antirheumatoid-drugs.adr: Methotrexate: mouth ulcers, bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, pneumonitis; sulfasalazine: GI upset and rash; hydroxychloroquine: retinopathy; leflunomide: liver injury and hypertension; TNF blockers: infections and reactivated tuberculosis
antirheumatoid-drugs.ci: Pregnancy (methotrexate, leflunomide, penicillamine); active infection and untreated tuberculosis (biologics); liver disease; bone marrow depression; G6PD deficiency (sulfasalazine, dapsone)

drugs-for-gout.moa: Acute attack: NSAIDs, colchicine (binds tubulin and stops neutrophil migration) and steroids; Chronic: allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit xanthine oxidase; probenecid and sulfinpyrazone block renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid (uricosurics); pegloticase breaks down uric acid
drugs-for-gout.uses: Colchicine and NSAIDs for the acute attack; allopurinol, febuxostat and probenecid for long-term uric acid lowering; allopurinol also in tumour lysis syndrome
drugs-for-gout.adr: Colchicine: diarrhoea, nausea, bone marrow suppression; allopurinol: rash, hypersensitivity syndrome, and an acute attack may be triggered at the start; probenecid: stones and GI upset; febuxostat: cardiovascular risk
drugs-for-gout.ci: Never start urate-lowering drugs during an acute attack; uricosurics in renal stones or poor renal function; allopurinol with azathioprine or mercaptopurine (reduce dose); colchicine in severe renal or hepatic disease

drugs-for-cough.moa: Demulcents soothe the pharynx; expectorants and mucolytics (bromhexine, ambroxol, acetylcysteine) loosen or thin bronchial secretions; antitussives suppress the cough centre (codeine, pholcodine, dextromethorphan) or act peripherally (benzonatate, levodropropizine)
drugs-for-cough.uses: Dry irritating cough: antitussives; productive cough: expectorants and mucolytics; allergic cough: antihistamines
drugs-for-cough.adr: Codeine: constipation, drowsiness, dependence; dextromethorphan: dizziness and, at high dose, hallucinations; antihistamine mixtures: sedation and dryness; ammonium salts: nausea
drugs-for-cough.ci: Opioid antitussives in asthma, respiratory depression, children under 2 years and with productive cough; avoid suppressing a cough when secretions need to be cleared

drugs-for-bronchial-asthma.moa: β2 agonists relax bronchial smooth muscle; theophylline inhibits phosphodiesterase and blocks adenosine; anticholinergics block vagal tone; leukotriene antagonists (montelukast, zafirlukast) block leukotriene receptors; mast cell stabilisers (sodium cromoglycate) stop mediator release; corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation; omalizumab binds IgE
drugs-for-bronchial-asthma.uses: Relievers: salbutamol, terbutaline, ipratropium in attacks; Controllers: inhaled corticosteroids, long-acting β2 agonists (salmeterol, formoterol), montelukast, theophylline; severe allergic asthma: omalizumab
drugs-for-bronchial-asthma.adr: β2 agonists: tremor, palpitations, hypokalaemia; theophylline: nausea, arrhythmias and seizures (narrow therapeutic index); inhaled steroids: oral candidiasis and hoarseness; oral steroids: usual systemic effects; montelukast: headache and neuropsychiatric effects
drugs-for-bronchial-asthma.ci: Non-selective β-blockers, aspirin and NSAIDs may trigger attacks; long-acting β2 agonists alone without an inhaled steroid; theophylline with arrhythmias, seizures or drugs that raise its level (erythromycin, ciprofloxacin)
